tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

title.description: Short noun-phrase title for the chapter (under 40 chars). Shown in the table of contents.

summary.description: Optional one-line summary of what this chapter covers. Shown on hover in the table of contents.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to pat@example.com' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__resize_window
tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

action.description: What to do. ERN_Memory_Model_Specification_v0.1.md
# Formalization design

Decisions for the Lean formalization. They govern how to formalize, never what ERN means: semantics comes only from `specs/`. Agents follow them. A design question not settled here is proposed in the report, never decided silently.

## Goal

Check that the spec's rules deliver what ERN promises. A rule that cannot be formalized or proven as written is a result: report it with the failing goal, never work around it.

Three results stay distinct: the formal model of the rules, the theorems proven about that model, and later the correctness of the compiler against it. This formalization covers the first two.

## Architecture

The formalization uses two permanent, complementary models linked
by a refinement theorem.

This is an architectural decision about formalization, not a
normative decision about ERN semantics. Both models must faithfully
represent the validated specifications.

If a specification cannot be represented faithfully, the mismatch
must be reported. Any necessary change to the formalization
architecture requires an explicit revision of this document.

1. **Abstract model.** Memory is a set of places: variables and field paths (`p.right`). Gives the semantics of safe code. States what safe code may assume about memory.
2. **Concrete model.** Memory is byte-addressed allocations. Gives the semantics of safe and unsafe code. Parameterized by a layout interface, never by a fixed layout.
3. **Refinement theorem.** Links the two models. It is the formal statement of ERN's safety promise.

## Concrete memory

- Bytes are abstract: each byte carries its initialization state and, when it belongs to a pointer, its provenance. Address and provenance are distinct.
- The concrete model represents every distinction the spec's rules rely on, including storage shared by several places.

## Layout interface

- Size, alignment and position of each component of a type are abstract functions.
- Their guarantees (in bounds, non-overlapping where the spec requires it, aligned) are hypotheses carried as structure fields or typeclass assumptions, never Lean `axiom`s.
- The interface contains only guarantees that some spec rule needs. Each hypothesis cites the rule that requires it.
- Non-vacuity: whenever the interface changes, a layout satisfying it is exhibited and proven. An unsatisfiable interface would make every refinement result empty.
- Realizability for every admissible target and instance is an obligation of the charter's ABI and layout step. It stays recorded as open until that step discharges it.

## Main theorems

- **Observable behaviors** are defined explicitly: termination with its observable result, trap, undefined behavior, divergence. Refinement compares concrete behaviors projected onto abstract observations.
- **Abstract safety.** A program accepted by the static rules has no undefined behavior in the abstract model.
- **Refinement.** For every layout satisfying the interface: if each unsafe region satisfies its contract, every observable behavior of an accepted program in the concrete model projects to a behavior of the abstract model. Concrete safety follows from abstract safety.
- **Unsafe contracts.** A contract is an entry condition and an exit condition relating the two models. From any state satisfying the entry condition, no execution of the region reaches undefined behavior, and every non-trap exit satisfies the exit condition. A trap is terminal: it runs no cleanup and is compared as an observable behavior. The relation between the models implies the entry condition of any region reachable from safe code; a stronger entry condition must be established by the unsafe code that enters the region. Intermediate states may break the relation, since in sequential execution no other code observes them. Under concurrency, shared state is observable during the region; the contract form for that case is decided before milestone 4.
- **Scope.** Every theorem states the language fragment it covers. A theorem on a fragment supports no claim about the whole language; sequential safety implies nothing about concurrent safety.

## Construction order

1. Control flow infrastructure: abstract syntax and operational semantics of control constructs. No safety theorem yet: the control flow spec's preservation rule depends on the memory and concurrency models.
2. Memory model, safe part, on the abstract model. Abstract safety for the sequential fragment.
3. Concrete model, layout interface and refinement for the sequential fragment. The memory model counts as verified for that fragment only once refinement is proven.
4. Concurrency model: extends both models and the refinement.
5. IR dialect, once its dependencies are formalized.

The semantic style of milestones 4 and 5 and their target theorems are decided here before they start.

## Representation

- **Abstract syntax** is built incrementally: only the constructs required by the rules being formalized. No concrete syntax.
- **Semantics** is a step function where the spec is deterministic, a step relation where it is not. Interpreters for tests iterate steps with fuel. Running out of fuel is not an outcome, neither termination nor trap. Each interpreter is proven to agree with the unbounded semantics on every result it returns.
- **No Mathlib** unless a milestone requires it. Adding it is a design decision recorded here.

**Why:** the briefs require French commit messages (one per step), docstrings citing `MM-0x.y` rules, statement changes justified in the report, and say `formal/reports/` is exploration never merged into `main`. Later briefs add "arbitrages" that answer earlier report questions.

**How to apply:** start a new pass from the latest branch tip; run an adversarial review workflow over module and report before delivering; `lake` is not on PATH, call `~/.elan/bin/lake`; keep the Lake library name `Ern`. `formal/Ern/.gitkeep` keeps showing as deleted: restore it with `git checkout`, never commit the deletion. A post-commit hook can make `git commit` exceed 2 minutes: give it a long timeout. The axiom rule ({propext, Quot.sound} only) forbids core lemmas that pull `Classical.choice` (`List.getElem?_mapIdx`, `List.eq_nil_iff_forall_not_mem`, `List.nodup_range`, `List.pairwise_lt_range`): sweep `#print axioms` over every theorem and replace them with local lemmas. Mathlib tactics (`set`, `tauto`) are unavailable. Reviews keep catching report errors: quote old forms from the old commit, count declarations with a command, and base an evidence claim only on a check that would fail on the defect. After fixing review findings, run a second targeted review of the fixes: in MM-03 pass 2 a fix over-rejected legitimate programs. Before calling a clause "missing" from an arbitrage, re-read every earlier arbitrage still in force: in pass 3 the clause needed for exitFrame_no_dangling was A4's root-holder rule, which A1 puts in WF3 and pass 2 had left out. `timeout` does not exist on this Mac: run `lake build` directly (about 2.5 min). When an arbitrage enlarges a definition used in hypotheses (pass 4: `Inv3` gained `NoDangling`), theorems whose text is unchanged silently narrow: give them only the conjunct they use. Before retiring a counterexample whose witness breaks a new invariant clause, look for another witness: pass-4 review found one and flagged the weakening as major. Check obligations against the initial state: the base frame of `S3.init` owns no place, so an obligation about it can be vacuous on reached states. A review fix can itself pick a semantic reading (pass 5: the kind conjunct of `IsInternalFor` rejected a `newArena` that D3 leaves undecided): check every fix for verdicts it changes on cases the text is silent on. Module docstrings must cite the report's own numbering, not the review's decision numbers. Arbiter-supplied theorems can be false: check them on small reached states (owned storage, a parameter that is the ancestor of another) before trying a proof. Every factual claim in the report needs a module witness, or reviewers flag it; never say "blocked until X" without checking escape sequences such as ending the owner value. When a precondition gains clauses, lemmas taking it as a hypothesis narrow silently: name the old precondition (pass 7: `EnterPreBase`) and give the lemmas only what they use. A guard on one operation (G2 on `store`) is usually bypassable through another (a helper authority then `release`/`endUse`/`free`/exit): look for such bypasses before claiming a configuration is excluded. A new check on an operation with a defined failure (`issue` → `fail`) must not turn that failure into `reject`. Use one adversarial reviewer per arbitrage lens; each found distinct real issues in pass 7. When a restriction rejects an old counterexample, try to rebuild a witness that satisfies the new clause before restating it as a rejection (pass 8: a same-shape destination restored `transfer_not_inv3_preserving`). Drop hypotheses a proof does not use. When cases disappear because their state is no longer reached, replay their verdicts on a new reachable state and list the drops. Machine-check every changed verdict the report lists, including the old witnesses' rejected steps. Never state "only clause X fails" as `X → Pre` next to `¬ X`: that is vacuous; name the other clauses (pass 8: `TransferPreBase` with an iff) and state them. Run a second targeted check after fixing verification findings: in pass 8 it caught that vacuous form. `omega` proving a conjunction goal pulls `Classical.choice`: split the goal first. `meta` is a keyword in this Lean: never name a hypothesis `meta`. `set` (Mathlib) is unavailable: use `obtain ⟨x, hx⟩ : ∃ x, x = e := ⟨_, rfl⟩`. `if_pos`/`if_neg`/`ite_cond_eq_true` are deprecated: use `simp only [h, ↓reduceIte]`. When `S3.Usable.mono` is applied with `rfl` for `hP`, give `(s := …) (s' := …)` explicitly or it unifies the wrong way. Simulation theorems: never quantify obligations over all translations (vacuous); put them as per-step premises of the run with parameters fixed once, and give a concrete multi-step run as witness. A universal encoding obligation (`∀ addr, decode (enc addr) = addr`) is unsatisfiable by a finite computable decode: state it per value. `lake env lean` uses the last built olean: rebuild the module before a scratch file uses new declarations. Never use an unquoted heredoc for Lean or docstrings: backticks run as shell commands; use `<<'EOF'` and pass paths by environment variable. `example`s escape a `collectAxioms` sweep: rename them to theorems in a scratch copy to check their axioms. `awk length` counts bytes, not characters: count line length in Python. Each check round finds errors in the previous round's wording: when a sentence is fixed in a docstring, grep the report for the same claim; quote arbitrages exactly (L2 said "hypothèse des énoncés", not "hors langage"); classify every item a deliverable asks to classify instead of moving it aside; a summary must not present a hypothesis restated in a conclusion as a result. Count theorem constants with internal ones (`isInternal`) and say which count you give. A callee cannot move a value out of a parameter's footprint (`ActiveDerivedOutside` counts the parameter itself): build values to transfer as callee locals. Authority ids shift with every alloc/issue/split: check them with `#eval` of `prun` prefixes before writing a case. A literal invariant from the material can fail under the full kernel extension: keep the literal statement with counterexamples and prove the parts that hold, under their own names. A runner's fallback state must be unreachable (e.g. no frame) or a statement "the run's state is reached" is vacuous when the run fails; give a lemma deriving success from reachability. Projecting `.2` out of an existential passes the elaborator but fails in the kernel: use `obtain`. When `step_ok_of`-style lemmas time out at `whnf`, pass the contract `k` and statics explicitly. Jalon 3 took four check rounds (11/9/9/4 confirmed): each round's fixes need their own narrow check. The list `Sublist` notation `<+` is scoped: write `List.Sublist`; `List.take_add` pulls `Classical.choice`. `omit … in` goes before the docstring. A `def` in a `variable (k : K)` section takes `k` only if it uses it: check call sites. In a multi-line `{ st with … }`, put each field on its own line at one column. Theorems stated for registered arenas (`ar ∈ s.arenas`) do not carry over to library instances: never cite them for one. Before writing "the only effect of X is Y", look for a witness in the other direction (derivability: the missing guard also turned a `fail` into an `ok`).

PR ernlang/ern#2 ready for review, not merged. Inter-spec boundaries: KExt (§42), §86 typing → Spec 4, MM3-H H16 → Spec 3, MM23-H16 → Spec 8 (address) + Spec 11 (width/encoding); the lowest-address rule is a non-normative reference realization, not §82.3. 449	# VI. Abstract Authority Machine
450	
451	The components described below constitute the logical state of the sequential discipline. They prescribe neither generalized runtime metadata nor reference syntax.
452	
453	## 38. Machine State
454	
455	The access discipline is based on the finite state
456	
457	\[ S_3=(F,P,I,A,D) \]
458	
459	where `F` represents the frame stack, `P` the places, `I` their initialization, `A` the authorities, and `D` the validity anchors. Administrative states of arenas and other library abstractions are separate from `S₃`. The external contract `K` is a separate parameter. The internal representation may carry auxiliary information that creates no new rights.
460	
461	## 39. Execution Frames
462	
463	`F` is a nonempty stack of identified, non-duplicate frames. Every frame except the initial frame knows its parent. Frames hold temporary authorities and directly local places. The **current frame** is at the top of the stack. `ancestor(f₁, f₂)` means `f₁` is `f₂` or an ancestor of `f₂` in the stack and its call chain.
464	
465	The base frame, whose identity is 0 in states reachable from the initial state, never exits. An exited frame can neither be the terminal owner of a usable place nor hold an authority that remains active. Frames have semantic existence; no particular runtime representation is required.
466	
467	## 40. Logical Places, Leaves, and Ownership
468	
469	A place has an identity, optionally a structural parent, an abstract `kind`, an owner `owner : Frame | Place`, and a logical death marker. Structural parenthood `partOf(p,q)` describes the subplaces of a value; `owner` describes **who keeps the storage** of a root place valid. An owned place may lie outside its owner's direct footprint; ownership and composition are therefore distinct.
470	
471	A **leaf** is a place with no structural children. `footprint(p)` contains the leaves of `p`, and access rights over a place are evaluated on those leaves. Places transitively owned by a value are not automatically leaves of its `footprint`. A logical unit of the access discipline does not automatically constitute an additional allocation in the elementary memory machine.
472	
473	A place `p` is **usable** (`Usable(s,p)`) if and only if:
474	
475	1. `p` exists and is not marked dead;
476	2. if its owner is a frame, that frame belongs to the stack;
477	3. if its owner is a place `q`, then `q` is itself usable and the chain terminates at a frame in the stack.
478	
479	An ownership cycle makes no place usable. `placeFrame(p)` is the terminal frame of this chain when `p` is usable. Structural parts share their parent's owner and death marker. A value may be logically ended by `endUse` without the place that contained it becoming unusable; the substorages it owned may, however, die.
480	
481	A **root place** has no structural parent. Every **usable** root place has a root authority of own mode `Modify`, with no origin, held exactly by that place's owner (`RootHeld`). This authority cannot be transferred in isolation; root ownership follows a legal transfer of the owning value when necessary.
482	
483	## 41. Leaf Initialization States
484	
485	Every tracked leaf has exactly one of the states `Uninit`, `Init`, or `Moved`.
486	
487	- `Uninit`: no initialized value available in this leaf.
488	- `Init`: initialized value, subject to type, representation, and storage obligations.
489	- `Moved`: value consumed by transfer, inaccessible as its former value.
490	
491	Aggregates may be partially initialized. Both `Uninit` and `Moved` prohibit ordinary reads, while remaining distinct states for diagnostics and end-of-use obligations. An initialization state creates no access permission.
492	
493	## 42. Authorities, Modes, Holders, and Origins
494	
495	An authority conceptually has the following fields:
496	
497	```text
498	Authority {
499	    id
500	    mode: Observe | Modify
501	    origin?: AuthorityId
502	    footprint: Set<Leaf>
503	    holder: Frame | Place
504	    active: Bool
505	}
506	```
507	
508	`origin` links a derived authority to its current origin. Authorities have fresh identities and well-formed origin chains. A root authority has no origin; a derived authority has one. Creating derived rights does not increase the scope or permitted mode of the origin.
509	
510	The **holder** (`holder`) is not the **owner** (`owner`). An authority derived by `derive` or `split` is initially held by the current frame; `store` or a permitted transfer may make it held by a place. The derived `issue` operation proceeds through `split` followed by `store`. `release` does not release a root. There is no persistent `Suspended` field: suspension of rights is inferred from active descendants and applies leaf by leaf.
511	
512	## 43. Effective Rights and Exercise of Authorities
513	
514	For an authority `a` and a leaf `l`, `effective(s,a,l)` is derived from the active descendants of `a` whose footprint contains `l`:
515	
516	1. if `a` is inactive or does not cover `l`, its effective mode is absent;
517	2. if no active descendant covers `l`, the effective mode is the own mode of `a`;
518	3. if an active descendant with own mode `Modify` covers `l`, the effective mode of `a` is absent;
519	4. otherwise, when the covering active descendants are `Observe`, the effective mode of `a` on `l` is `Observe`.
520	
521	The effect is **local to each leaf**: after splitting a region, the origin may retain effective `Modify` over undistributed leaves.
522	
523	Requested modes are ordered `Observe ≤ Modify`. `ExercisableAt(s,a,m)` means:
524	
525	- `a` is active and its own mode permits `m`;
526	- either `a` is held by the current frame;
527	- or `a` is held by a place `p`, and the current frame has, over **all** leaves of `p`, an authority itself exercisable in mode `m` with sufficient effective mode.
528	
529	The latter clause is recursive along the holder chain. Thus, being active or covering a leaf does not automatically make an authority exercisable. `HasRight(s,m,p)` means the current frame has exercise in mode `m` and sufficient effective mode **over every leaf in `p`'s footprint**. Every operation requires the modes it actually needs; an authority's own mode alone is insufficient.
530	
531	## 44. Dependencies and Effective Anchors
532	
533	`D(p)` is the set of authorities serving as **validity anchors** for place `p`. An anchor is valid as long as the authority it names is active. Dependencies of contained values are accounted for transitively. Relevant dependencies follow the value during transfer; those of its container do not automatically follow a part transferred in isolation.
534	
535	For an authority `x`, its **effective anchor** is the root reached by traversing its origin chain. It does not necessarily coincide with its current holder. Lifetime constraints are calculated from the frame of that effective anchor and the frames of places that remain usable. A dependency cannot create a right or artificially extend a lifetime.
536	
537	`AnchorOrder` requires, for every anchor `x ∈ D(q)` of a usable place `q`, that the frame of the effective anchor of `x` be the frame of `q` or one of its ancestors. `AnchorOrderHeld` imposes the same rule on every **active authority held** by `q`. These conditions apply to the resulting states of operations that move or create holder relations.
538	
539	## 45. Parameters, Returns, and Reanchoring
540	
541	A call parameter is an **active derived authority held by the caller** before being passed to the callee; its original provenance may go back to an earlier frame. This interpretation does not require that the authority was originally derived in the calling frame; that additional requirement belongs to Spec 3. The caller **yields** the authority to the new frame: it does not simultaneously retain a copy. If the authority remains in that frame upon return, `exitFrame` releases it; **it is not automatically returned to the caller**. To retain its own right, the caller may pass a **fresh derivative** of the authority it wishes to keep: this is ordinary reborrowing. The definition of ergonomic calling conventions is deferred to Spec 3.
542	
543	A result is returned by a legal `transfer` into the result place provided by the caller as a `Modify` parameter. Surviving authorities and their dependencies are reanchored by `exitFrame` to still-valid origins. There is no standalone correspondence `M` and no implicit escape permission.
544	
545	## 46. Arenas as Library Administration States
546	
547	Each entry belongs to the library's abstract state, **separate from kernel state `S₃`**. It has the following fields:
548	
549	```text
550	ArenaEntry {
551	    storage: PlaceId
552	    internal: AuthorityId
553	    available: Set<Leaf>
554	    issued: Set<(Region, AuthorityId)>
555	}
556	```
557	
558	A region is **available if and only if each of its leaves belongs to `available`**; the empty region is always available. Issuance removes the leaves of the issued region from `available`. Reset restores all leaves of the administered storage to that set. The registry and its updates belong to the abstraction contract and create no kernel permissions.
559	
560	The arena is **live** if `internal` is active. The **arena value** is the place holding `internal`, distinct from the possible owner of `storage`. Administered storage may be local, static, allocated, or issued by another arena, under `newArena` preconditions and applicable invariants. `available` and `issued` remain **in the library's arena entry**.
561	
562	## 47. Initial State
563	
564	The kernel's initial state contains only base frame 0 and the declared static storage. Every static leaf has its declared initial state, `Init` or `Uninit`. The roots of static places directly owned by frame 0 have a root `Modify` authority held by that frame; a static may also be owned by another static, in which case its root authority is held by the latter. The ownership graph of statics is acyclic: no static is owned, directly or transitively, by itself. The initial state invents no dynamic allocation, derived authority, or implicit anchor. The initial arena registry belongs to library state and is empty. The initial frame does not exit.
565	
566	## 48. External Parametric Contract
567	
568	`K` contains the predicates `DeclaredDisjoint`, `SharedMutable`, `Pinned`, `ExternalDone`, `Deallocable`, `FreeCompat`, and `Satisfiable`. Their obligations are specified in Section 80. `K` can neither fabricate access rights nor remove an obligation of the Charter. The predicate `Invalidates` is not part of this contract.
569	
570	# VII. Invariants of Reachable States
571	
572	Machine states are subject to structural, validity, and exclusivity requirements preserved by permitted transitions under their declared external contracts.
573	
574	## 49. WF3 — Well-Formedness of Frames, Places, and Authorities
575	
576	`WF3(s)` is a **predicate on state `s`**. It jointly requires:
577	
578	1. a nonempty, duplicate-free frame stack, every frame having a valid identity and, except for the base frame, a valid parent; frame-parent relations are well-founded;
579	2. a place structure whose composition links are valid and **acyclic**; every structural part shares its parent's owner and death marker;
580	3. valid owners of type frame or place, and **well-founded** ownership chains reaching a live frame for every usable place;
581	4. footprints consisting exclusively of leaves of existing places;
582	5. authorities with valid identities and modes, whose existing origins form **acyclic** chains ending at a root authority;
583	6. `RootChain`: every origin chain of an authority covering a leaf ends at the root of the **same structural root place** as that leaf;
584	7. `RootHeld`: every usable root place has its active root `Modify` authority, with no origin, held exactly by its owner;
585	8. holder validity: every active authority is held by a frame present in the stack or by a usable place.
586	
587	Numerical ordering of identifiers, parent precedence over child in a list, and bounds on generated identifiers may be used **to represent or prove** this well-formedness in a formalization; they are not normative restrictions on place or authority identities. Preservation of `WF3` by a transition is a **required property of transitions**, not an additional clause of the state predicate. `WF3` does not impose any particular physical object layout: that belongs to refinement into the elementary memory machine.
588	
589	## 50. I1 — Structural Exclusivity
590	
591	For two active authorities **unrelated by derivation** covering the same leaf, their own modes must both be `Observe`. This rule also applies to leaves identified as `SharedMutable`; their particular mutation is governed by the `writeShared` contract and creates no exception to I1.
592	
593	Exclusivity of **effective** modes (`effective_exclusive`) is a consequence of I1 and the definition of `effective`, not the definition of I1. On a leaf, two incompatible authorities cannot simultaneously possess incompatible effective rights. The only permitted independent ordinary coexistence is `Observe` / `Observe`.
594	
595	## 51. I2 — Conservation of Rights
596	
597	A derived authority covers only a subfootprint of what its origin chain permits and does not elevate its mode. Derivation and splitting restrictions do not allow duplication of an exclusive right over a leaf. Every active authority is linked to a valid origin according to state and reanchoring rules: an origin is **valid** if and only if it is active, so the origin of an active derived authority is active. Partial suspension follows from `effective`.
598	
599	## 52. I3 — Validity of Anchors and Dependencies
600	
601	Every explicit anchor of a still-usable place is valid. An operation cannot invalidate an anchor retained by a place that remains usable. Transitive propagation of dependencies from contained values does not change this obligation. Dependencies are not permissions and are insufficient to justify an access.
602	
603	## 53. I4 — Consumption and Movement
604	
605	A `Moved` leaf cannot be read as if it still contained its previous value. Moving a value does not preserve two copies of an exclusive authority. Initialization state and authority-exercise state are separate checks.
606	
607	## 54. Anchor Ordering and Absence of Orphan Rights
608	
609	`AnchorOrder` and `AnchorOrderHeld` are defined in Section 44. `NoDangling` prohibits an **active** authority from covering a leaf belonging to an unusable place; the invariant does not say that a leaf is initialized. `NoOrphan` requires every active authority held by a place to be connected to a frame in the stack through a **finite, non-repeating chain** of authorities: the first link is held by a live frame, and each active link **structurally covers the entirety** of the place holding the next link. The link need not have an effective mode over that place. `NoOrphan` guarantees neither the exercisability of all stored authorities nor freedom from blocking.
610	
611	## 55. ArenaInv — Invariant of the Arena Abstraction
612	
613	`ArenaInv` is an invariant of the **library contract**, not an additional predicate of kernel state. For every live arena:
614	
615	- `storage` designates an existing, usable place; the footprint of `internal` is exactly the footprint of `storage`;
616	- `internal` is active, with own mode `Modify`, held by the arena value;
617	- available leaves and issued regions belong to the administered storage;
618	- two still-active issuances have disjoint regions; no leaf of a still-issued region simultaneously belongs to `available`;
619	- every still-issued block authority is a derivative of `internal` complying with exclusivity and validity rules;
620	- anchor and ownership restrictions are respected.
621	
622	Arena entries do not, by themselves, constitute an additional storage owner. Two live arenas may cover common leaves when their `internal` authorities are distinct and their effective rights are compatible; no **global** disjointness of arena footprints is imposed.
623	
624	## 56. Uniqueness of Live Administration
625	
626	**An authority identity may serve as `internal` for at most one live administrative abstraction**, whether an arena, `HandlePool`, `DataStack`, or another library administrative instance. Before registering a new abstraction, its creation operation must jointly check the absence of that identity from **all relevant registries of live administrations**. Uniqueness concerns the identity of the `internal` authority, not merely possible overlap of footprints: abstractions with distinct `internal` identities are not forbidden merely because their footprints overlap. Library contracts must make the information required for this guard available to the creation operation; checking only an abstraction's own registry is insufficient.
627	
628	**This guard is not a condition for any safety property in Section 57.** The effective right (Section 43, case 3) already prohibits a second issuance over leaves covered by an active block derived from the same authority. Rather, the guard preserves the **abstraction contract**: without it, simultaneous administration of the same `internal` could cause `reject` instead of `fail`, or reissue a previously released block that the first administration still considers unavailable. It creates neither permissions nor allocations and introduces no general detection of authority cycles. Its physical representation and encapsulation of library registries remain outside the kernel.
629	
630	## 57. Main Invariant
631	
632	\[
633	Inv3 = I1 \land I2 \land I3 \land I4 \land AnchorOrder \land NoDangling
634	\]
635	
636	On states reachable from `S3.init statics` under `DDSound(K)`, the kernel guarantees:
637	
638	\[
639	WF3 \land Inv3 \land AnchorOrderHeld \land NoOrphan
640	\]
641	
642	`ArenaInv` (Section 55) belongs to the library abstraction: it is not included in this main kernel invariant.
643	
644	**I5:** every pinned leaf, statically (`K.Pinned`) or dynamically (an active pinning obligation, Section 74), belongs to a usable place.
645	
646	I5, associated with pinned storage, remains a **specialized obligation** of `K.Pinned`, not a clause automatically implied by sequential accesses alone. This property is required for reachable states under the declared assumptions. Its correspondence with allocations and bytes requires the refinement defined below.
647	
648	# VIII. Definition of Transitions and Management of Authorities
649	
650	The following operations are abstract transition rules. They distinguish rejection by the discipline, defined failure, and a permitted transition.
651	
652	## 58. Transition Outcomes
653	
654	Every operation has a conceptual outcome among:
655	
656	```text
657	Outcome3 = ok(new_state) | reject | fail
658	```
659	
660	`reject` means that the static discipline does not permit the step; it is neither an implicit runtime trap nor `ub` in the elementary memory machine. `fail` is a **defined failure** leaving the state unchanged; **only `alloc` may produce it in the O1–O16 kernel**. Other kernel operations produce `ok` or `reject`. Library-abstraction operations, including `issue` (§77), may define their own `fail` cases. Where such failure is provided, static preconditions are checked before dynamic availability, according to the operation's contract.
661	
662	An `ok` transition must satisfy its preconditions, apply exactly its prescribed effects, and preserve the relevant invariants. No transition fabricates a permission to make its conclusion true. Holder and anchor changes are evaluated in the **resulting state** when a rule explicitly so provides.
663	
664	## 59. Implicit Preservation of Modes and Anchors
665	
666	Changes in effective authority are **derived** from active authorities and their origins; no `Suspended` indicator is mutated. Access operations (O9–O11) do not change an anchor without an explicitly authorized effect of transfer, `depend`, `store`, release, or reanchoring. Leaves becoming `Init` do so through a permitted write (`write3`, `writeShared`, `store`, including during a derived `issue`) or a transfer from a corresponding source leaf already `Init`; leaves initialized in `S3.init` are declared as such.
667	
668	## 60. O1 — Derivation of an Authority
669	
670	**Preconditions**
671	
672	1. `source` is an active derived or root authority, and `ExercisableAt(s,source,mode)` holds; its origin chain and anchors are valid: every authority of its origin chain, its effective anchor included, is active.
673	2. The leaves of `region` exist and belong to the footprint of `source`; `mode` does not exceed the available effective right on these leaves.
674	3. The addition preserves exclusivity I1: no unrelated active authority becomes incompatible with the derived right, and already-active descendants are respected.
675	4. The new holding frame is the live current frame. The admissible state's footprint and anchoring restrictions remain true.
676	
677	**`ok` effect:** A new active authority with fresh identity, origin `source`, requested mode and footprint, and held by the current frame is added. The source remains active; its effective modes are recomputed per leaf. No storage or place anchor is created. Multiple compatible observations remain permitted. **Other outcome:** `reject`.
678	
679	## 61. O2 — Splitting Authorities
680	
681	**Preconditions**
682	
683	1. `source` is active and exercisable by the current frame with sufficient modification rights over the relevant leaves.
684	2. Each region lies within the available, effectively modifiable footprint of the source.
685	3. Regions are pairwise disjoint under structural composition or contract `K.DeclaredDisjoint`, subject to obligation `DDSound(K)`; no exclusive right already distributed is overlapped.
686	4. Creation of the derivatives respects origins, conservation I1/I2, and validity obligations.
687	
688	**`ok` effect:** An active derived `Modify` authority held by the current frame is created for each region. `source` remains active; its effective modification capability disappears only over distributed leaves and remains on undistributed leaves. Authorities are split logically: `split` performs no physical allocation. **Other outcome:** `reject`.
689	
690	An unjustified declaration of disjointness may invalidate the proof: without `DDSound`, an accepted `split` may violate I1. Constructing zero-sized subregions is not identified with an allocation of the elementary memory machine; the case of an empty shape in `alloc` is distinct.
691	
692	## 62. O3 — End of a Derived Borrow
693	
694	**Preconditions**
695	
696	1. `authority` is active **and derived**: an authority with no origin is rejected.
697	2. It is held by the current frame, or by a place `p` on which the current frame has exercisable `Modify`.
698	3. No active descendant of the authority prevents its release; no other still-usable value may lose a required anchor.

# VI. Abstract Authority Machine

The components described below constitute the logical state of the sequential discipline. They prescribe neither generalized runtime metadata nor reference syntax.

## 38. Machine State

The access discipline is based on the finite state

\[ S_3=(F,P,I,A,D) \]

where `F` represents the frame stack, `P` the places, `I` their initialization, `A` the authorities, and `D` the validity anchors. Administrative states of arenas and other library abstractions are separate from `S₃`. The external contract `K` is a separate parameter. The internal representation may carry auxiliary information that creates no new rights.

## 39. Execution Frames

`F` is a nonempty stack of identified, non-duplicate frames. Every frame except the initial frame knows its parent. Frames hold temporary authorities and directly local places. The **current frame** is at the top of the stack. `ancestor(f₁, f₂)` means `f₁` is `f₂` or an ancestor of `f₂` in the stack and its call chain.

The base frame, whose identity is 0 in states reachable from the initial state, never exits. An exited frame can neither be the terminal owner of a usable place nor hold an authority that remains active. Frames have semantic existence; no particular runtime representation is required.

## 40. Logical Places, Leaves, and Ownership

A place has an identity, optionally a structural parent, an abstract `kind`, an owner `owner : Frame | Place`, and a logical death marker. Structural parenthood `partOf(p,q)` describes the subplaces of a value; `owner` describes **who keeps the storage** of a root place valid. An owned place may lie outside its owner's direct footprint; ownership and composition are therefore distinct.

A **leaf** is a place with no structural children. `footprint(p)` contains the leaves of `p`, and access rights over a place are evaluated on those leaves. Places transitively owned by a value are not automatically leaves of its `footprint`. A logical unit of the access discipline does not automatically constitute an additional allocation in the elementary memory machine.

A place `p` is **usable** (`Usable(s,p)`) if and only if:

1. `p` exists and is not marked dead;
2. if its owner is a frame, that frame belongs to the stack;
3. if its owner is a place `q`, then `q` is itself usable and the chain terminates at a frame in the stack.

An ownership cycle makes no place usable. `placeFrame(p)` is the terminal frame of this chain when `p` is usable. Structural parts share their parent's owner and death marker. A value may be logically ended by `endUse` without the place that contained it becoming unusable; the substorages it owned may, however, die.

A **root place** has no structural parent. Every **usable** root place has a root authority of own mode `Modify`, with no origin, held exactly by that place's owner (`RootHeld`). This authority cannot be transferred in isolation; root ownership follows a legal transfer of the owning value when necessary.

## 41. Leaf Initialization States

Every tracked leaf has exactly one of the states `Uninit`, `Init`, or `Moved`.

- `Uninit`: no initialized value available in this leaf.
- `Init`: initialized value, subject to type, representation, and storage obligations.
- `Moved`: value consumed by transfer, inaccessible as its former value.

Aggregates may be partially initialized. Both `Uninit` and `Moved` prohibit ordinary reads, while remaining distinct states for diagnostics and end-of-use obligations. An initialization state creates no access permission.

## 42. Authorities, Modes, Holders, and Origins

An authority conceptually has the following fields:

```text
Authority {
    id
    mode: Observe | Modify
    origin?: AuthorityId
    footprint: Set<Leaf>
    holder: Frame | Place
    active: Bool
}
```

`origin` links a derived authority to its current origin. Authorities have fresh identities and well-formed origin chains. A root authority has no origin; a derived authority has one. Creating derived rights does not increase the scope or permitted mode of the origin.

The **holder** (`holder`) is not the **owner** (`owner`). The derived `issue` operation proceeds through `split` followed by `store`. `release` does not release a root. ## 43. Effective Rights and Exercise of Authorities

Requested modes are ordered `Observe ≤ Modify`. `ExercisableAt(s,a,m)` means:

- `a` is active and its own mode permits `m`;
- either `a` is held by the current frame;
- or `a` is held by a place `p`, and the current frame has, over **all** leaves of `p`, an authority itself exercisable in mode `m` with sufficient effective mode.

Every operation requires the modes it actually needs; an authority's own mode alone is insufficient.

The definition of ergonomic calling conventions is deferred to Spec 3.

## 46. Arenas as Library Administration States

Each entry belongs to the library's abstract state, **separate from kernel state `S₃`**. It has the following fields:

```text

    internal: AuthorityId

Reset restores all leaves of the administered storage to that set. The registry and its updates belong to the abstraction contract and create no kernel permissions.

Administered storage may be local, static, allocated, or issued by another arena, under `newArena` preconditions and applicable invariants. `available` and `issued` remain **in the library's arena entry**.

## 47. Initial State

The kernel's initial state contains only base frame 0 and the declared static storage. Every static leaf has its declared initial state, `Init` or `Uninit`. The roots of static places directly owned by frame 0 have a root `Modify` authority held by that frame; a static may also be owned by another static, in which case its root authority is held by the latter. The ownership graph of statics is acyclic: no static is owned, directly or transitively, by itself. The initial state invents no dynamic allocation, derived authority, or implicit anchor. The initial arena registry belongs to library state and is empty. The initial frame does not exit.

`K` contains the predicates `DeclaredDisjoint`, `SharedMutable`, `Pinned`, `ExternalDone`, `Deallocable`, `FreeCompat`, and `Satisfiable`. Their obligations are specified in Section 80. `K` can neither fabricate access rights nor remove an obligation of the Charter. The predicate `Invalidates` is not part of this contract.

## 52. I3 — Validity of Anchors and Dependencies

Every explicit anchor of a still-usable place is valid. An operation cannot invalidate an anchor retained by a place that remains usable. Transitive propagation of dependencies from contained values does not change this obligation. Dependencies are not permissions and are insufficient to justify an access.

## 53. I4 — Consumption and Movement

A `Moved` leaf cannot be read as if it still contained its previous value. Moving a value does not preserve two copies of an exclusive authority. Initialization state and authority-exercise state are separate checks.

## 54. Anchor Ordering and Absence of Orphan Rights

`AnchorOrder` and `AnchorOrderHeld` are defined in Section 44. `NoDangling` prohibits an **active** authority from covering a leaf belonging to an unusable place; the invariant does not say that a leaf is initialized. `NoOrphan` requires every active authority held by a place to be connected to a frame in the stack through a **finite, non-repeating chain** of authorities: the first link is held by a live frame, and each active link **structurally covers the entirety** of the place holding the next link. The link need not have an effective mode over that place. `NoOrphan` guarantees neither the exercisability of all stored authorities nor freedom from blocking.

## 55. ArenaInv — Invariant of the Arena Abstraction

`ArenaInv` is an invariant of the **library contract**, not an additional predicate of kernel state. For every live arena:

- `storage` designates an existing, usable place; the footprint of `internal` is exactly the footprint of `storage`;
- `internal` is active, with own mode `Modify`, held by the arena value;
- available leaves and issued regions belong to the administered storage;
- two still-active issuances have disjoint regions; no leaf of a still-issued region simultaneously belongs to `available`;
- every still-issued block authority is a derivative of `internal` complying with exclusivity and validity rules;
- anchor and ownership restrictions are respected.

Arena entries do not, by themselves, constitute an additional storage owner. Two live arenas may cover common leaves when their `internal` authorities are distinct and their effective rights are compatible; no **global** disjointness of arena footprints is imposed.

## 56. Uniqueness of Live Administration

**An authority identity may serve as `internal` for at most one live administrative abstraction**, whether an arena, `HandlePool`, `DataStack`, or another library administrative instance. Before registering a new abstraction, its creation operation must jointly check the absence of that identity from **all relevant registries of live administrations**. Uniqueness concerns the identity of the `internal` authority, not merely possible overlap of footprints: abstractions with distinct `internal` identities are not forbidden merely because their footprints overlap. Library contracts must make the information required for this guard available to the creation operation; checking only an abstraction's own registry is insufficient.

**This guard is not a condition for any safety property in Section 57.** The effective right (Section 43, case 3) already prohibits a second issuance over leaves covered by an active block derived from the same authority. Rather, the guard preserves the **abstraction contract**: without it, simultaneous administration of the same `internal` could cause `reject` instead of `fail`, or reissue a previously released block that the first administration still considers unavailable. It creates neither permissions nor allocations and introduces no general detection of authority cycles. Its physical representation and encapsulation of library registries remain outside the kernel.

## 57. Main Invariant

\[
Inv3 = I1 \land I2 \land I3 \land I4 \land AnchorOrder \land NoDangling
\]

On states reachable from `S3.init statics` under `DDSound(K)`, the kernel guarantees:

\[
WF3 \land Inv3 \land AnchorOrderHeld \land NoOrphan
\]

`ArenaInv` (Section 55) belongs to the library abstraction: it is not included in this main kernel invariant.

**I5:** every pinned leaf, statically (`K.Pinned`) or dynamically (an active pinning obligation, Section 74), belongs to a usable place.

I5, associated with pinned storage, remains a **specialized obligation** of `K.Pinned`, not a clause automatically implied by sequential accesses alone. This property is required for reachable states under the declared assumptions. Its correspondence with allocations and bytes requires the refinement defined below.

# VIII. Definition of Transitions and Management of Authorities

The following operations are abstract transition rules. They distinguish rejection by the discipline, defined failure, and a permitted transition.

## 58. Transition Outcomes

Every operation has a conceptual outcome among:

```text
Outcome3 = ok(new_state) | reject | fail
```

`reject` means that the static discipline does not permit the step; it is neither an implicit runtime trap nor `ub` in the elementary memory machine. `fail` is a **defined failure** leaving the state unchanged; **only `alloc` may produce it in the O1–O16 kernel**. Other kernel operations produce `ok` or `reject`. Library-abstraction operations, including `issue` (§77), may define their own `fail` cases. Where such failure is provided, static preconditions are checked before dynamic availability, according to the operation's contract.

An `ok` transition must satisfy its preconditions, apply exactly its prescribed effects, and preserve the relevant invariants. No transition fabricates a permission to make its conclusion true. Holder and anchor changes are evaluated in the **resulting state** when a rule explicitly so provides.

## 59. Implicit Preservation of Modes and Anchors

Changes in effective authority are **derived** from active authorities and their origins; no `Suspended` indicator is mutated. Access operations (O9–O11) do not change an anchor without an explicitly authorized effect of transfer, `depend`, `store`, release, or reanchoring. Leaves becoming `Init` do so through a permitted write (`write3`, `writeShared`, `store`, including during a derived `issue`) or a transfer from a corresponding source leaf already `Init`; leaves initialized in `S3.init` are declared as such.

## 60. O1 — Derivation of an Authority

**Preconditions**

1. `source` is an active derived or root authority, and `ExercisableAt(s,source,mode)` holds; its origin chain and anchors are valid: every authority of its origin chain, its effective anchor included, is active.
2. The leaves of `region` exist and belong to the footprint of `source`; `mode` does not exceed the available effective right on these leaves.
3. The addition preserves exclusivity I1: no unrelated active authority becomes incompatible with the derived right, and already-active descendants are respected.
4. The new holding frame is the live current frame. The admissible state's footprint and anchoring restrictions remain true.

**`ok` effect:** A new active authority with fresh identity, origin `source`, requested mode and footprint, and held by the current frame is added. The source remains active; its effective modes are recomputed per leaf. No storage or place anchor is created. Multiple compatible observations remain permitted. **Other outcome:** `reject`.

## 61. O2 — Splitting Authorities

**Preconditions**

1. `source` is active and exercisable by the current frame with sufficient modification rights over the relevant leaves.
2. Each region lies within the available, effectively modifiable footprint of the source.
3. Regions are pairwise disjoint under structural composition or contract `K.DeclaredDisjoint`, subject to obligation `DDSound(K)`; no exclusive right already distributed is overlapped.
4. Creation of the derivatives respects origins, conservation I1/I2, and validity obligations.

**`ok` effect:** An active derived `Modify` authority held by the current frame is created for each region. `source` remains active; its effective modification capability disappears only over distributed leaves and remains on undistributed leaves. Authorities are split logically: `split` performs no physical allocation. **Other outcome:** `reject`.

An unjustified declaration of disjointness may invalidate the proof: without `DDSound`, an accepted `split` may violate I1. Constructing zero-sized subregions is not identified with an allocation of the elementary memory machine; the case of an empty shape in `alloc` is distinct.

## 62. O3 — End of a Derived Borrow

**Preconditions**

1. `authority` is active **and derived**: an authority with no origin is rejected.
2. It is held by the current frame, or by a place `p` on which the current frame has exercisable `Modify`.
3. No active descendant of the authority prevents its release; no other still-usable value may lose a required anchor.

4. If the authority is stored in its holding place, that place is exempted from the check “this authority still appears among the anchors” **only because the effect removes that anchor at the same time**. An anchor with the same identity attached by `depend` to another usable place continues to block the step.
